title: Chapter 106 — Ahab’s Leg
paragraphs: The hasty manner in which Captain Ahab had left the Samuel Enderby of London had not been without some small violence to his own person. He had landed with such energy upon a thwart of his boat that his ivory leg had received a half-splintering shock. And when, after gaining his own deck and his own pivot-hole there, he so vehemently wheeled round with an urgent command to the steersman — it was, as ever, something about his not steering firmly enough — then the already shaken ivory received such an additional twist and wrench that, though it still remained intact and to all appearances strong, Ahab did not consider it entirely trustworthy.

And indeed it seemed hardly surprising that, for all his pervading, mad recklessness, Ahab did at times pay careful attention to the condition of that dead bone on which he partly stood. For not very long before the Pequod sailed from Nantucket, he had been found one night lying face-down on the ground, unconscious: by some unknown and seemingly inexplicable, unimaginable accident, his ivory limb had been so violently displaced that it had struck him like a stake and all but pierced his groin; and only with extreme difficulty was the agonizing wound entirely healed.

Nor, at the time, had it failed to enter his monomaniac mind that all the anguish of that present suffering was nothing but the direct result of an earlier woe. And he seemed to see all too plainly that just as the most poisonous reptile of the marsh perpetuates its kind as inevitably as the sweetest songbird of the grove, so, equally with every happiness, all miserable events naturally beget their like. Yes, more than equally, thought Ahab, since both the ancestry and the descendants of Grief reach further than the ancestry and descendants of Joy. For, leaving aside this point — that it is an inference from certain church teachings that while some natural pleasures here will have no children born to them in the other world, but, on the contrary, will be followed by the joy-childlessness of all hell's despair, some guilty mortal miseries will still fruitfully beget for themselves an eternally growing brood of griefs beyond the grave — leaving that aside entirely, there still seems to be an inequality in the deeper analysis of the thing. For, thought Ahab, while even the highest earthly happiness always has a certain meaningless pettiness lurking in it, all heart-woes have at bottom a mystic significance, and in some men an archangelic grandeur; and careful tracing-out of them does not contradict the obvious conclusion. To trace the family trees of these high mortal miseries leads us at last among the sourceless first-born lines of the gods; so that, in the face of all the glad, haymaking suns and the soft, cymbal-clashing round harvest moons, we must give in to this: that the gods themselves are not forever glad. The ineradicable, sad birthmark on the brow of man is only the stamp of sorrow in those who signed it.

Unwittingly here a secret has been divulged which perhaps might more properly have been disclosed before, in due order. Along with many other particulars concerning Ahab, it had always remained a mystery to some why, for a certain period both before and after the sailing of the Pequod, he had hidden himself away with such grand-lama-like seclusion, and for that one interval sought speechless refuge, as it were, among the marble senate of the dead. Captain Peleg's rumored reason for this seemed by no means adequate, though indeed, where all Ahab's deeper nature was concerned, every revelation partook more of significant darkness than of explanatory light. But in the end it all came out — this one matter did, at least. That dreadful mishap was at the bottom of his temporary seclusion. And not only this, but to that ever-shrinking, dwindling circle ashore who, for any reason, possessed the privilege of a less prohibited approach to him — to that timid circle the above-hinted accident, remaining as it did moodily unexplained by Ahab, invested itself with terrors not entirely unrelated to the land of spirits and of wails. So that, through their concern for him, they had all conspired, so far as they could, to hush up the knowledge of this thing from others. And hence it was that not till a considerable time had passed did it come to light upon the Pequod's decks.

But be all this as it may; whether or not the unseen, ambiguous council in the air, or the vindictive princes and potentates of fire, have anything to do with earthly Ahab, in this present matter of his leg he took plain, practical steps: he called the carpenter.

And when that functionary appeared before him, he ordered him to set about making a new leg without delay, and directed the mates to see that he was supplied with all the studs and joists of jaw-ivory (Sperm Whale) accumulated so far on the voyage, so that a careful selection of the stoutest, clearest-grained stuff could be made. This done, the carpenter received orders to have the leg finished that night, and to provide all the fittings for it, independent of those belonging to the distrusted one in use. Moreover, the ship's forge was ordered to be hoisted out of its temporary idleness in the hold; and, to speed things up, the blacksmith was commanded to begin at once forging whatever iron contrivances might be needed.
